title: حِكَايَةُ عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ مَعَ شَمْسِ النَّهَارِ
titleEn: ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār
part: Night 158 · ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 779–780 (Night 158, continuing directly from nights-157), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 158 continues the tale of ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār. Abū al-Ḥasan brings Shams al-Nahār's slave-girl to ʿAlī's house; ʿAlī revives at the sight of her and reads the letter she carries. It opens with a short poem and goes on in rhymed prose, a letter "written without fingers, spoken without a tongue", on sleepless eyes, a body worn out and a love that only grows, with two more pieces of verse set into it. ʿAlī sends back his greeting and a plea for rescue from the sea of ruin, weeps with the girl, and Abū al-Ḥasan sees her off and goes back to his shop. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الثَّامِنَةُ وَالْخَمْسُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-thāminatu wa-al-khamsūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the eighth-and-fifty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and fifty-eighth night,
sentences.n: al-thāmina, “the eighth”, is the ordinal, feminine to agree with layla; al-khamsūn, “fifty”, keeps its cardinal form and is joined by wa-. The alif of المائة is not pronounced: the word is miʾa.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ أَبَا الْحَسَنِ ذَهَبَ بِالْجَارِيَةِ إِلَى دَارِ عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ وَأَوْقَفَهَا عَلَى الْبَابِ وَدَخَلَ الْبَيْتَ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna Abā al-Ḥasani dhahaba bi-al-jāriyati ilā dāri ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin wa-awqafahā ʿalā al-bābi wa-dakhala al-bayta
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that Abū al-Ḥasan went with the slave-girl to the house of ʿAlī son of Bakkār, and stood-her at the door, and entered the house.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that Abū al-Ḥasan took the slave-girl to the house of ʿAlī ibn Bakkār, left her standing at the door, and went inside.
sentences.n: As each night opens, Shahrazād repeats where the last one stopped: Night 157 closed with Abū al-Ḥasan leaving the girl at ʿAlī's door. Abā al-Ḥasani is accusative after anna; abū, “father”, becomes abā. dhahaba bi-, “to go with”, is “to take (someone) along”. awqafa, “to make stand” (Form IV of waqafa).

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأٰهُ عَلِيُّ ابْنُ بَكَّارٍ فَرِحَ بِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾāhu ʿAliyyu ibnu Bakkārin fariḥa bihi
sentences.l: And when ʿAlī son of Bakkār saw-him, he-rejoiced at-him.
sentences.i: When ʿAlī ibn Bakkār saw him, he was glad.
sentences.n: The print writes raʾāhu, “he saw him”, as رأه, without the second alif; the long vowel is shown here with a dagger alif. The object comes before the subject: “saw him ʿAlī”. Here the print spells the name ابن with its alif (ibn), where a few words earlier it wrote بن; both are “son”. fariḥa bi-, “to rejoice at”: the verb chooses bi- for the cause of the joy.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ أَبُوالْحَسَنِ سَبَبُ مَجِيئِي أَنَّ فُلَانًا أَرْسَلَ إِلَيْكَ جَارِيَتَهُ بِرُقْعَةٍ تَتَضَمَّنُ سَلَامَهُ عَلَيْكَ وَذَكَرَ فِيهَا أَنَّ سَبَبَ تَأَخُّرِهِ عَنْكَ لِعُذْرٍ حَصَلَ لَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu Abū al-Ḥasani sababu majīʾī anna fulānan arsala ilayka jāriyatahu bi-ruqʿatin tataḍammanu salāmahu ʿalayka wa-dhakara fīhā anna sababa taʾakhkhurihi ʿanka li-ʿudhrin ḥaṣala lahu
sentences.l: And Abū al-Ḥasan said to-him: The cause of my-coming (is) that so-and-so has sent to-you his-slave-girl with a-note (that) contains his-greeting upon-you; and he-mentioned in-it that the cause of his-delay from-you (is) for an-excuse (that) befell him.
sentences.i: Abū al-Ḥasan said to him, “I have come because So-and-so has sent you his slave-girl with a note carrying his greetings, in which he says that he has been kept from you by something that came up.
sentences.n: Abū al-Ḥasan speaks for the ears of ʿAlī's household: the cover story makes the girl the servant of some male friend, fulān, “so-and-so”, the word for a person one does not name. ابوالحسن is printed as one word again. ruqʿa, “a scrap, a note”, a short letter. tataḍammanu, “which contains” (Form V of ḍamina): a clause describing the indefinite ruqʿatin, with no relative word. salāmahu ʿalayka, “his greeting upon you”: the greeting is said to fall “upon” the one greeted. anna sababa taʾakhkhurihi … li-ʿudhrin, “that the cause of his delay is for an excuse”: the li- of cause repeats what sabab already says, a loose colloquial build. ʿudhr is “an excuse, a hindrance one can plead”. The hamzas of مجيئي and تأخره are the print's own.

sentences.t: وَالْجَارِيَةُ وَاقِفَةٌ بِالْبَابِ فَهَلْ تَأْذَنُ لَهَا بِالدُّخُولِ
sentences.tr: wa-al-jāriyatu wāqifatun bi-al-bābi fa-hal taʾdhanu lahā bi-al-dukhūli
sentences.l: And the slave-girl (is) standing at the door; so do you-give-leave to-her for the entering?
sentences.i: The girl is standing at the door; will you let her come in?”
sentences.n: wa-al-jāriyatu wāqifatun, “and the girl (is) standing”: a sentence with no verb, its predicate an active participle. adhina li- … bi-, “to give someone leave to do something”: li- marks the one permitted, bi- what is permitted. The hamza of تأذن is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ عَلِيٌّ أَدْخِلُوهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla ʿAliyyun adkhilūhā
sentences.l: And ʿAlī said: Make-enter-her.
sentences.i: ʿAlī said, “Bring her in.”
sentences.n: adkhilū, “make (her) enter, bring in”, Form IV of dakhala, is a plural imperative: ʿAlī gives the order to his household, not to Abū al-Ḥasan alone. The print's bare alif carries no hamza; it is supplied.

sentences.t: فَغَمَزَهُ أَبُوالْحَسَنِ أَنَّهَا جَارِيَةُ شَمْسِ النَّهَارِ فَعَرَفَ بِالْإِشَارَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-ghamazahu Abū al-Ḥasani annahā jāriyatu Shamsi al-Nahāri fa-ʿarafa bi-al-ishārati
sentences.l: And Abū al-Ḥasan winked-at-him that she (is) the slave-girl of Shams al-Nahār, and he-knew by the sign.
sentences.i: Abū al-Ḥasan gave him a wink to say that she was Shams al-Nahār's slave-girl, and ʿAlī understood the sign.
sentences.n: ghamaza, “to press, to wink”, takes the person signalled to as its object (-hu), and annahā … says what the wink conveyed. ʿarafa, “to know”, here “to grasp, understand”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأٰهَا تَحَرَّكَ وَفَرِحَ وَقَالَ لَهَا بِالْإِشَارَةِ كَيْفَ حَالُ السَّيِّدِ شَفَاهُ اللَّهُ وَعَافَاهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾāhā taḥarraka wa-fariḥa wa-qāla lahā bi-al-ishārati kayfa ḥālu al-sayyidi shafāhu Allāhu wa-ʿāfāhu
sentences.l: And when he-saw-her, he-stirred and rejoiced, and said to-her by the sign: How (is) the state of the master, may God heal-him and restore-him?
sentences.i: When he saw her he stirred and brightened, and asked her by signs, “How is the master, God heal him and make him well?”
sentences.n: raʾāhā is again printed without its second alif (رأها) and pointed with a dagger alif. ʿAlī asks by gesture because the household is present, and says al-sayyid, “the master”, masculine, to keep up the fiction: he means Shams al-Nahār. shafāhu Allāhu wa-ʿāfāhu: perfect verbs used as a wish, “may God heal him and grant him well-being”; ʿāfā, Form III, is “to grant ʿāfiya, health”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ بِخَيْرٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat bi-khayrin
sentences.l: And she-said: In good.
sentences.i: She said, “Well.”
sentences.n: bi-khayrin, “in good (state)”: the everyday answer to “how is …?”, “(he is) well”, with the subject left unsaid.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَخْرَجَتِ الْوَرَقَةَ وَدَفَعَتْهَا لَهُ فَأَخَذَهَا وَقَبَّلَّهَا وَفَتَحَهَا وَقَرَأَهَا وَنَاوَلَهَا لِأَبِى الْحَسَنِ فَوَجَدَ مَكْتُوبًا فِيهَا هَذِةِ الْأَبْيَاتُ
sentences.tr: thumma akhrajati al-waraqata wa-dafaʿathā lahu fa-akhadhahā wa-qabbalahā wa-fataḥahā wa-qaraʾahā wa-nāwalahā li-Abī al-Ḥasani fa-wajada maktūban fīhā hādhihi al-abyātu
sentences.l: Then she-brought-out the paper and handed-it to-him, and he-took-it and kissed-it and opened-it and read-it and passed-it to Abū al-Ḥasan; and he-found written in-it (were) these verses:
sentences.i: Then she brought out the letter and handed it to him. He took it, kissed it, opened it and read it, and passed it to Abū al-Ḥasan, who found these verses written in it:
sentences.n: The print sets its shadda over the lām of قبلّها; the doubling belongs to the bāʾ, qabbala, “to kiss” (Form II), and the print's mark is kept where it stands, beside the one supplied. akhrajati takes a linking -i before al-. dafaʿa li-, “to hand to”: li- marks the receiver, where Classical prefers ilā. nāwala, “to pass, hand over” (Form III), takes li- the same way; abū becomes abī after li-, and the print writes it with ى (لابى). wajada maktūban fīhā hādhihi al-abyātu, “he found written in it these verses”: maktūban is the object of wajada, and the verses are taken as the subject of the participle, “written (were) these verses”; one could also read al-abyāta as the object with maktūban describing it, and the bare print does not decide. The print spells hādhihi with ة (هذة), its habit. The hamza of قرأها is the print's own.

sentences.t:
يُنْبِيكَ هٰذَا الرَّسُوْلُ عَنْ خَبَرِى * فَاسْتَغْنِ فِيْ ذِكْرِهِ عَنِ النَّظَرِ
خَلَفْتَ صَبًّا بِحُبِّكُمْ شَغَفًا * وَطَرْفُهُ لَايَزَالُ بِالسَّهَرِ
أُكَابِدُ الصَّبْرَ فِى الْبَلَاءِ فَمَا * يَدْفَعُ خَلْقٌ مَوَاقِعَ الْقَدَرِ
وَقَرِّ عَيْنًا فَلَيْسَ تَغْفَلُ عَنْ * قَلْبِيْ وَلَا يَوْمَ غِبْتَ عَنْ بَصَرِى
وَانْظُرْ إِلَى جِسْمِكَ النَّحِيلِ وَمَا * قَدْ حَلَّهُ وَاسْتَدِلِّ بِالْاَثَرِ
sentences.tr:
yunbīka hādhā al-rasūlu ʿan khabarī * fa-istaghni fī dhikrihi ʿani al-naẓari
khalafta ṣabban bi-ḥubbikum shaghafan * wa-ṭarfuhu lā yazālu bi-al-sahari
ukābidu al-ṣabra fī al-balāʾi fa-mā * yadfaʿu khalqun mawāqiʿa al-qadari
wa-qarri ʿaynan fa-laysa taghfalu ʿan * qalbī wa-lā yawma ghibta ʿan baṣarī
wa-unẓur ilā jismika al-naḥīli wa-mā * qad ḥallahu wa-istadilli bi-al-athari
sentences.l:
This messenger will-inform-you of my-news, * so dispense, in his-telling, with the looking.
You-have-left-behind a-lover, with-love-of-you (one) passion-struck, * and his-eye does-not-cease in the wakefulness.
I-wrestle-with patience in the affliction, for not * does a-creature ward-off the fallings of the decree.
And be-cool of eye, for not are-you-heedless of * my-heart, and not a-day were-you-absent from my-sight.
And look at your-body, the wasted, and what * has alighted-on-it, and take-as-proof the trace.
sentences.i:
This messenger will tell you all my news, so his telling will serve you in place of seeing me.
You left behind a lover sick with love of you, whose eyes never stop their watching through the night.
I labour on in patience through my trial, for no creature can turn aside the blows that fate lets fall.
Be comforted: you are never out of my heart's thoughts, nor were you absent from my sight a single day.
Look at your own wasted body and what has come upon it, and from that trace infer my state.
sentences.n: The metre is munsariḥ. The pointing is the print's own except الى in the last line, which the print leaves bare and which is pointed here (ilā). The poem is Shams al-Nahār's, written to ʿAlī; the girl who carries it is “this messenger”. yunbīka is yunbiʾuka, “informs you” (Form IV of nabaʾa), with the hamza softened to a long ī, as verse and later Arabic often do. istaghni ʿan, “to do without”: his account will spare ʿAlī the need to see her. khalafta is pointed as Form I; the sense “you left behind” is more usually Form II, khallafta, and either scans. ṣabb, “a lover”, and shaghafan, “in passion”, an accusative saying in what way; shaghaf is love that reaches the heart's membrane (shaghāf). bi-ḥubbikum, “with love of you”: the plural -kum is the polite plural, meaning ʿAlī alone. The print runs lā yazālu together (لَايَزَالُ), and the long vowels of الرَّسُوْلُ, فِيْ and قَلْبِيْ carry a sukūn, a habit of its verse pointing. The fourth line is uncertain. ghafala ʿan is “to be heedless of, to neglect”, and taghfalu can be “you” or “she”. Read as “you”, the words say “you are not heedless of my heart”; the rendering here takes them as “you are never out of my heart's thoughts”, which suits the next half-line but strains the verb. Read as “she”, the subject would be the eye of qarri ʿaynan. Neither reading is certain. qarra ʿaynan, “be cool of eye”, is “be comforted”: a cool eye is a happy one, a hot eye one that weeps. In the last line Shams al-Nahār tells ʿAlī to read her suffering from his own wasted body; istadalla bi-, “to take as evidence”, and athar, “a trace, a mark left behind”.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدُ فَقَدْ كَتَبْتُ لَكَ كِتَابًا بِغَيْرِ بَنَانٍ * وَنَطَقْتُ لَكَ بِغَيْرِ لِسَانٍ *
sentences.tr: wa-baʿdu fa-qad katabtu laka kitāban bi-ghayri banānin * wa-naṭaqtu laka bi-ghayri lisānin *
sentences.l: And after: then I-have written to-you a-writing without fingertips, * and I-spoke to-you without a-tongue. *
sentences.i: And now to my purpose. I have written you a letter with no fingers to write it, and spoken to you with no tongue to speak.
sentences.n: The letter turns from its opening verses to prose, and the prose is rhymed (sajʿ): banān and lisān close the two clauses, and the print marks each close with a star. wa-baʿdu, “and after”: the letter-writer's formula for passing from the greeting to the business, short for ammā baʿdu; baʿdu is indeclinable in -u when what it is “after” is left unsaid. fa-qad katabtu, “then I have written”: fa- follows naturally after baʿdu. banān, “fingertips”: the conceit is that her love, not her hand, has written, and the page speaks for her as a tongue would; or that she is too wasted to have hand or tongue left. bi-ghayri, “without”: bi-, “with”, + ghayr, “other than”.

sentences.t: وَجُمْلَةُ شَرْحِ حَالِي أَنَّ لِي عَيْنًا لَايُفَارِقُهَا السَّهَرُ * وَقَلْبًا لَاتَبْرَحُ مِنْهُ الْفِكَرُ *
sentences.tr: wa-jumlatu sharḥi ḥālī anna lī ʿaynan lā yufāriquhā al-saharu * wa-qalban lā tabraḥu minhu al-fikaru *
sentences.l: And the sum of the explaining of my-state (is) that for-me (is) an-eye, wakefulness does-not leave-it, * and a-heart, the thoughts do-not depart from-it. *
sentences.i: The whole account of my state is this: I have an eye that sleeplessness never leaves, and a heart that cares never quit.
sentences.n: The print runs lā and the verb together in لايفارقها and لاتبرح; the spacing is kept. anna lī ʿaynan, “that to me is an eye”: lī, “to me”, is how Arabic says “I have”, and the noun after it is accusative because anna governs it; qalban is accusative by the same anna. Each noun is described by a clause with no relative word, as usual after an indefinite. al-fikar, “thoughts, cares”, is the plural of fikra; the verb tabraḥu is feminine because the subject is a plural of things. sahar and fikar make the rhyme.

sentences.t: فَكَأَنَّنِي قَطُّمَا عَرَفْتُ صِحَّةً * وَلَا فَارَقْتُ تَرْحَةً * وَلَارَأَيْتُ مَنْظَرًا بَهِيًّا * وَلَا قَطَعْتُ عَيْشًا هَنِيًّا * وَكَأَنَّنِي خُلِقْتُ مِنَ الصَّبَابَةِ * وَمِنْ أَلَمِ الْوَجْدِ وَالْكَآبَةِ *
sentences.tr: fa-kaʾannanī qaṭṭu mā ʿaraftu ṣiḥḥatan * wa-lā fāraqtu tarḥatan * wa-lā raʾaytu manẓaran bahiyyan * wa-lā qaṭaʿtu ʿayshan haniyyan * wa-kaʾannanī khuliqtu mina al-ṣabābati * wa-min alami al-wajdi wa-al-kaʾābati *
sentences.l: So as-if-I ever not-knew health, * and-not parted (from) sorrow, * and-not saw a-sight bright, * and-not passed a-life pleasant; * and as-if-I was-created from ardour, * and from the pain of passion and dejection. *
sentences.i: It is as though I had never known health, nor ever been parted from sorrow, nor seen a lovely sight, nor passed a pleasant life; as though I had been made of love's ardour, and of the pain of passion and of gloom.
sentences.n: The print runs qaṭṭu and mā together (قطما), and lā and raʾaytu together (ولارأيت); the spacing is kept, and the hamza of رأيت is the print's own. qaṭṭu, “ever, at all”, goes with a negated past: here it comes before the negative mā, and the following lā … lā carry the same “never” on. kaʾannanī, “as if I”: kaʾanna with the pronoun -nī. tarḥa, “sorrow, grief”, is the opposite of faraḥ, “joy”. qaṭaʿa ʿayshan, “to cut a life”, i.e. to pass it. haniyyan stands for hanīʾan, “pleasant, wholesome”: the print writes هنيا without hamza, and the hamza is read as a doubled yāʾ, which also makes the rhyme with bahiyyan. The rhyme then moves to ṣabāba, “ardour of love”, and kaʾāba, “dejection”, whose madda is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَعَلَيَّ السَّقَامُ مُتَرَادِفٌ * وَالْغَرَامُ مُتَضَاعِفٌ * وَالشَّوْقُ مُتَكَاثِرٌ * وَالْوَجْدُ بِقَلْبِي ثَايِرٌ *
sentences.tr: fa-ʿalayya al-saqāmu mutarādifun * wa-al-gharāmu mutaḍāʿifun * wa-al-shawqu mutakāthirun * wa-al-wajdu bi-qalbī thāyirun *
sentences.l: So upon-me sickness (is) coming-one-after-another, * and passion (is) doubling, * and longing (is) multiplying, * and ardour in-my-heart (is) rising-up. *
sentences.i: Sickness comes on me wave upon wave, my passion doubles, my longing multiplies, and love's fever rages in my heart.
sentences.n: Four short sentences without a verb, each a subject and a participle as predicate; the first puts ʿalayya, “upon me”, in front. The shadda of فعليّ is the print's own. mutarādif, “following close one on another” (Form VI of radifa); mutaḍāʿif, “doubling”, and mutakāthir, “multiplying”, are Form VI participles too, chosen partly for the jingle. thāyir stands for thāʾir, “stirred up, raging”: the print writes ثاير, with the hamza turned into a yāʾ glide as in speech.

sentences.t: وَصِرْتُ كَمَا قَالَ الشَّاعِرُ *
sentences.tr: wa-ṣirtu ka-mā qāla al-shāʿiru *
sentences.l: And I-have-become as what the poet said: *
sentences.i: I have become as the poet said:
sentences.n: ṣirtu, “I became”, from ṣāra, a verb of becoming. ka-mā, “as”: ka-, “like”, + mā, “what”. al-shāʿir, “the poet”, carries on the rhyme of mutakāthir and thāyir, and the star leads into the verses.

sentences.t:
اَلْقَلْبُ مُنْقَبِضٌ وَالْفِكْرُ مُنْبَسِطٌ * وَالْعَيْنُ سَاهِرَةٌ وَالْجِسْمُ مَتْعُوْبُ
وَالصَّبْرُ مُنْفَصِلٌ وَالْهَجْرُ مُتَّصِلٌ * وَالْعَقْلُ مُخْتَبِلٌ وَالْقَلْبُ مَسْلُوبُ
sentences.tr:
al-qalbu munqabiḍun wa-al-fikru munbasiṭun * wa-al-ʿaynu sāhiratun wa-al-jismu matʿūbu
wa-al-ṣabru munfaṣilun wa-al-hajru muttaṣilun * wa-al-ʿaqlu mukhtabilun wa-al-qalbu maslūbu
sentences.l:
The heart (is) contracted and the thought (is) spread-out, * and the eye (is) wakeful and the body (is) wearied;
And patience (is) cut-off and estrangement (is) joined-on, * and the mind (is) deranged and the heart (is) stolen.
sentences.i:
My heart is clenched and my thoughts run everywhere, my eye keeps watch and my body is worn out;
Patience is cut off and estrangement never ends, my reason is distracted and my heart is stolen away.
sentences.n: Metre: basīṭ. Each hemistich is two short sentences, a noun and a participle, set in pairs of opposites: munqabiḍ, “contracted, gloomy”, against munbasiṭ, “spread out” (here the thoughts that wander everywhere); munfaṣil, “cut off”, against muttaṣil, “joined, continuous”. matʿūb, “wearied”, is a spoken-Arabic participle of taʿiba, “to tire”, where Classical has mutʿab; the print's sukūn on its wāw is kept. mukhtabil, “deranged”, Form VIII of khabala. The rhyme is -ūbu.

sentences.t: وَاعْلَمْ أَنَّ الشَّكْوَى * لَاتُطْفِى نَارَ الْبَلْوَى * لَكِنَّهَا تُعَلِّلُ مَنْ أَعَلَّهُ الِاشْتِيَاقُ * وَأَتْلَفَهُ الْفِرَاقُ *
sentences.tr: wa-iʿlam anna al-shakwā * lā tuṭfī nāra al-balwā * lākinnahā tuʿallilu man aʿallahu al-ishtiyāqu * wa-atlafahu al-firāqu *
sentences.l: And know that complaint * does-not extinguish the fire of affliction; * but-it diverts whom longing has-made-sick, * and parting has-destroyed-him. *
sentences.i: Know that complaining does not put out the fire of affliction; yet it eases one whom longing has made sick and parting has undone.
sentences.n: lā tuṭfī stands for lā tuṭfiʾu, “does not extinguish”: the print writes لاتطفى, run together and with the final hamza dropped, so the verb is read like a weak verb ending in -ī. shakwā and balwā make the first rhyme, ishtiyāq and firāq the second. tuʿallilu, Form II of ʿalla, “to divert, console (with hopes)”, and aʿallahu, Form IV, “made him ill”: a play on two forms of one root, the comfort and the sickness; the shaddas of تعلّل and اعلّه are the print's own. man, “whoever, the one whom”, is the object of tuʿallilu, and -hu in aʿallahu and atlafahu points back to it.

sentences.t: وَأَتَسَلَّى بِذِكْرِ لَفْظِ الْوِصَالِ * وَمَا أَحْسَنَ قَوْلَ مَنْ قَالَ *
sentences.tr: wa-atasallā bi-dhikri lafẓi al-wiṣāli * wa-mā aḥsana qawla man qāla *
sentences.l: And I-console-myself with mention of the word of union; * and how beautiful (is) the saying of who said: *
sentences.i: And I comfort myself by speaking the very word “union”; and how well the poet put it:
sentences.n: atasallā, “I console myself”, Form V of salā, takes bi- for what one is consoled with. wiṣāl, “union”, the lovers' meeting, is the opposite of firāq. mā aḥsana …, “how fine is …!”: the exclamation pattern mā afʿala, with its object in the accusative (qawla). wiṣāl and qāl rhyme.

sentences.t: اِذَالَمْ يَكُنْ فِى الْحُبِّ سُخْطٌ وَلَا رِضًى * فَايْنَ حَلَاوَاتُ الرَّسَائِلِ وَالْكُتْبِ
sentences.tr: idhā lam yakun fī al-ḥubbi sukhṭun wa-lā riḍan * fa-ayna ḥalāwātu al-rasāʾili wa-al-kutbi
sentences.l: If there-is not in love anger and-not contentment, * then where (are) the sweetnesses of the messages and the letters?
sentences.i: If love held neither anger nor goodwill, where would be the sweetness of messages and letters?
sentences.n: Metre: ṭawīl. The print sets idhā and lam as one word (اذالم), and writes فاين without a hamza; the verse is copied as printed. lam yakun …, “there was not …”: kāna with no predicate means “to exist”. sukhṭ, “displeasure, anger”, and riḍan, “contentment”, are the quarrels and reconciliations that give letters their savour. kutb is kutub, “letters, writings”, shortened for the metre. These verses end Shams al-Nahār's letter.

sentences.t: قَالَ أَبُوالْحَسَنِ فَلَمَّا قَرَأْتُهَا هَيَّجَتْ أَلْفَاظُهَا بَلَابِلِي وَأَصَابَتْ مَعَانِيهَا مَقَاتِلِي
sentences.tr: qāla Abū al-Ḥasani fa-lammā qaraʾtuhā hayyajat alfāẓuhā balābilī wa-aṣābat maʿānīhā maqātilī
sentences.l: Abū al-Ḥasan said: And when I-read-it, its-words stirred-up my-cares, and its-meanings struck my-mortal-spots.
sentences.i: Abū al-Ḥasan said: When I read it, its words stirred up all my cares, and its meanings struck me to the heart.
sentences.n: Here the tale turns for a moment to Abū al-Ḥasan's own telling, in the first person. ابوالحسن is again printed as one word. The hamza and the damma of قرأتُها are the print's own; -hā is the letter (waraqa, feminine). hayyaja, “to stir up, excite” (Form II). balābil, “cares, anxieties”, a plural of balbala. maqātil, “the mortal places”, the points of the body where a wound kills, plural of maqtal; to strike someone's maqātil is to wound him past healing. balābilī and maqātilī rhyme, though the print sets no star.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ دَفَعْتُهَا إِلَى الْجَارِيَةِ فَلَمَّا أَخَذَتْهَا قَالَ لَهَا عَلِيُّ بْنُ بَكَّارٍ أَبْلِغِي سَيِّدَتَكِ سَلَامِي وَعَرِّفِيهَا بِوَجْدِي وَغَرَامِي وَامْتِزَاجِ الْمَحَبَّةِ بِلَحْمِي وَعِظَامِي
sentences.tr: thumma dafaʿtuhā ilā al-jāriyati fa-lammā akhadhathā qāla lahā ʿAliyyu ibnu Bakkārin ablighī sayyidataki salāmī wa-ʿarrifīhā bi-wajdī wa-gharāmī wa-imtizāji al-maḥabbati bi-laḥmī wa-ʿiẓāmī
sentences.l: Then I-handed-it to the slave-girl; and when she-took-it, ʿAlī son of Bakkār said to-her: Convey (to) your-lady my-greeting, and make-her-know of my-ardour and my-passion, and the mingling of love with my-flesh and my-bones.
sentences.i: Then I handed it to the slave-girl, and when she had taken it ʿAlī ibn Bakkār said to her, “Give your lady my greetings, and tell her of my longing and my passion, and of how love has mingled with my flesh and my bones.
sentences.n: abligh, “convey!” (Form IV), here feminine ablighī, takes two objects, the person (sayyidataki, “your lady”) and the thing (salāmī). ʿarrafa bi-, “to inform of” (Form II): the verb chooses bi- for what is made known, and bi- governs all three nouns after it, wajdī, gharāmī and imtizāji. imtizāj, “mingling” (Form VIII of mazaja), and its own bi-, “with”. The speech runs on in rhyme: gharāmī and ʿiẓāmī.

sentences.t: وَأَخْبِرِيهَا أَنَّنِي مُحْتَاجٌ إِلَى مَنْ يُنْقِذُنِي مِنْ بَحْرِ الْهَلَاكِ وَيُنَجِّينِي مِنْ هَذَا الِارْتِبَاكِ
sentences.tr: wa-akhbirīhā annanī muḥtājun ilā man yunqidhunī min baḥri al-halāki wa-yunajjīnī min hādhā al-irtibāki
sentences.l: And inform-her that-I (am) in-need of whoever rescues-me from the sea of perdition and saves-me from this entanglement.
sentences.i: Tell her that I need someone to rescue me from the sea of ruin and deliver me from this distress.
sentences.n: akhbirī, “inform!” (Form IV, feminine), with -hā, “her”. muḥtāj ilā, “in need of”: the participle takes ilā. man, “one who”, here indefinite: “someone who would rescue me”. yunqidhunī, Form IV, “he rescues me”, and yunajjīnī, Form II, “he saves me”. irtibāk, “entanglement, perplexity” (Form VIII of rabaka), rhymes with halāk, “perdition”.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ تَعَدَّى عَلَيَّ الزَّمَانُ بِنَوَائِبِهِ فَهَلْ مِنْ مُنْجِدٍ يُخَلِّصُنِي مِنْ شَوَائِبِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-qad taʿaddā ʿalayya al-zamānu bi-nawāʾibihi fa-hal min munjidin yukhalliṣunī min shawāʾibihi
sentences.l: And Time has transgressed upon-me with its-calamities; so is-there any helper (who) frees-me from its-taints?
sentences.i: Fortune has wronged me with its blows; is there anyone at all to come to my help and free me from its troubles?”
sentences.n: taʿaddā ʿalā, “to overstep against, wrong” (Form V); the shadda of تعدّى is the print's own. al-zamān, “time”, is the fickle fortune of the poets. nawāʾib, “calamities”, plural of nāʾiba; shawāʾib, “impurities, taints”, plural of shāʾiba, here the ills time mixes into life; both rhyme, and their hamza is the print's own. hal min munjidin, “is there any helper?”: min before an indefinite in a question means “any at all”. yukhalliṣunī, “who will free me” (Form II), describes munjid without a relative word.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ بَكَى فَبَكَتِ الْجَارِيَةُ لِبُكَائِهِ وَوَدَّعَتْهُ وَخَرَجَتْ مِنْ عِنْدِهِ
sentences.tr: thumma bakā fa-bakati al-jāriyatu li-bukāʾihi wa-waddaʿathu wa-kharajat min ʿindihi
sentences.l: Then he-wept, and the slave-girl wept for his-weeping, and she-bade-him-farewell and went-out from his-presence.
sentences.i: Then he wept, and the slave-girl wept to see him weep; she took her leave of him and went out from his presence.
sentences.n: li-bukāʾihi, “because of his weeping”: li- gives the cause; the hamza of بكائه is the print's own. waddaʿa, “to bid farewell” (Form II), takes a direct object; its shadda is the print's own. min ʿindihi, “from beside him”.

sentences.t: وَخَرَجَ أَبُوالْحَسَنِ مَعَهَا وَوَدَّعَهَا فَانْصَرَفَتْ إِلَى حَالِهَا وَذَهَبَ أَبُوالْحَسَنِ إِلَى دُكَّانِهِ وَفَتَحَهَا وَجَلَسَ مِثْلَ عَادَتِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-kharaja Abū al-Ḥasani maʿahā wa-waddaʿahā fa-inṣarafat ilā ḥālihā wa-dhahaba Abū al-Ḥasani ilā dukkānihi wa-fataḥahā wa-jalasa mithla ʿādatihi
sentences.l: And Abū al-Ḥasan went-out with-her and bade-her-farewell; and she-went-off to her-state; and Abū al-Ḥasan went to his-shop and opened-it and sat like his-habit.
sentences.i: Abū al-Ḥasan went out with her and said goodbye to her, and she went her way; and he went to his shop, opened it, and sat there as he always did.
sentences.n: The narration is back in the third person: the “I” of Abū al-Ḥasan's telling has slipped away without notice, a common thing in the Nights. inṣarafat ilā ḥālihā, “she went off to her state”, i.e. about her own business. fataḥahā, “he opened it”: the pronoun is feminine, so dukkān, “shop”, is treated as feminine here, as it often is in the spoken language. mithla ʿādatihi, “like his habit”: an adverbial accusative.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she ceased the speech allowed her.
